Johannine Prologue
joh-HAN-yn PROH-log
proper noun
The opening eighteen verses of the Gospel of John (John 1:1–18); Johannine, pertaining to the apostle John; prologue, Greek prologos, a foreword.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Johannine Prologue is the opening of the fourth Gospel, John 1:1–18, one of the loftiest passages in all Scripture, in which the apostle declares the eternal deity of the Word, His agency in creation, His incarnation, and His revelation of the Father. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God—eternal, personal, distinct from the Father yet Himself fully God. All things were made by Him, and without Him was not anything made that was made; the Word is the Creator, not a creature. In Him was life, and the life was the light of men; the light shines in darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not. Then the great mystery: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth. He came unto His own, and His own received Him not; but to as many as received Him, He gave power to become the sons of God. The Prologue closes by declaring that no man has seen God at any time, but the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him. The dictionary reads the Johannine Prologue as the bedrock of orthodox Christology: the eternal Word, true God and true man, the Creator made flesh to reveal the Father and bring grace and truth.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The opening of John’s Gospel (John 1:1–18); the eternal deity of the Word, His agency in creation, His incarnation, and His revelation of the Father.

JOHANNINE PROLOGUE, the opening of the fourth Gospel (John 1:1–18).

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God.

All things were made by Him; the Word is Creator, not creature.

The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth.

The only begotten Son has declared the unseen Father.

📖 Key Scripture

Joh 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

Joh 1:3 — "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made."

Joh 1:14 — "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."

Joh 1:18 — "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Arians and their heirs mistranslate “the Word was God” to make Christ “a god”; the grammar and the whole Prologue confess the Word as true and eternal God.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to answer is the old Arian denial of the Word’s full deity, pressed today by the Jehovah’s Witnesses in their rendering “the Word was a god.” But the Greek will not bear it: the Word was with God (distinct in Person) and the Word was God (one in essence); and the Prologue at once adds that all things were made by Him—the Creator of all is no creature. To make the Word a lesser, created god is to overthrow the very gospel the Prologue announces, for only true God made flesh could declare the Father and bring grace and truth.

The principle to recover is the orthodox confession of the eternal Word made flesh. The Word is eternal—in the beginning was the Word; personal—the Word was with God; divine—the Word was God; the Creator—all things were made by Him; and incarnate—the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. This is the bedrock of Nicea and Chalcedon and of all sound Christology: true God and true man in one Person, the only begotten Son who has declared the unseen Father.
